Bauhaus colour palettes

Source: R/palettes.R
bauhaus_palette.Rd

bauhaus_palette() returns colours from a dial's palettes as a character vector. pal_bauhaus() and pal_bauhaus_c() return palette functions in the style of the scales package, for use with ggplot2::discrete_scale(), ggplot2::continuous_scale() or a theme's palette.* settings.

Usage

bauhaus_palette(
  dial = "turquoise",
  n = NULL,
  type = c("discrete", "sequential"),
  reverse = FALSE
)

pal_bauhaus(dial = "turquoise", reverse = FALSE)

pal_bauhaus_c(dial = "turquoise", reverse = FALSE)

Arguments

dial

A dial name. Case, spaces, hyphens and underscores are ignored, so "Signal Blue", "signal-blue" and "signal_blue" all work. See bauhaus_dial_names().

n

Number of colours. For the discrete palette at most 8; defaults to all 8. For the sequential palette any number; defaults to 7.

type

"discrete" or "sequential".

reverse

If TRUE, reverse the order of the colours.

Value

bauhaus_palette() returns a character vector of hex colours. pal_bauhaus() returns a discrete palette function of n; pal_bauhaus_c() returns a continuous palette function of values in [0, 1].

Details

Every dial has two palettes:

  • Discrete (8 colours): the dial's own signature colour and ink first, then accents borrowed from the other dials of the screensaver, picked to stand out against this dial's plate.

  • Sequential: a smooth ramp built from the dial's own colours. On light dials it runs from the daylight lume through the signature colour to the hour-numeral ink; on dark dials it rises from just above the plate, through the minute-track ink, to the numeral ink.

See also

scale_colour_bauhaus_d() and friends to use the palettes in a plot.

Examples

bauhaus_palette("turquoise")
#> [1] "#007C84" "#D31C3F" "#9B7C00" "#004F5D" "#5D6195" "#00753E" "#970000"
#> [8] "#152D55"
bauhaus_palette("ocean", n = 3)
#> [1] "#6AF4D9" "#FFC800" "#F9BB97"
bauhaus_palette("salmon", type = "sequential", n = 5)
#> [1] "#F6FFE9" "#E79472" "#BA0F01" "#851B04" "#531A03"

pal <- pal_bauhaus("yellow")
pal(4)
#> [1] "#BA0E01" "#0072B8" "#4A0305" "#00753E"

ramp <- pal_bauhaus_c("glacier")
ramp(c(0, 0.5, 1))
#> [1] "#F4FFFB" "#2E5B73" "#1B3A49"
